text: I won’t repeat what’s already been said in the comments. I’ll mention something rarely brought up: living abroad lets you strip away all the good and bad conditions of your original family and come back to yourself to see who you really are and how you can stand on your own in this world.
So true!!! Only by completely breaking away from your original environment and noise can you truly realize what kind of person you want to become.
As a clear minority group living abroad, you come to understand the necessity of respecting diversity and don’t believe any civilization is superior to others.
Trueeee!
I think the biggest value is just being able to survive no matter what.
A perfect summary of middle-class study abroad insights.
Learn early that no one is coming.
Clicked because when you want to find support, you think, don’t lose to this moment.
Another important thing: learning to cook haha. After being abroad for years and coming back, I found most friends still can’t really cook.
Abroad feels like a vacuum in the evaluation system—you temporarily leave the domestic system but haven’t yet entered theirs.
Such an accurate comment, it feels like you’re building your own standards of evaluation during studying abroad.
Here’s something else: I only realized after going abroad for school that you can actually rest at home when you’re sick.
I can do everything on my own, nothing can scare me anymore about being alone.
Studying abroad brings the ability to live independently, self-learning, self-management, a global perspective, and critical thinking.
You start learning to recognize yourself, separating your true self from others, achieving spiritual freedom.
You become more tolerant.
My only skill now might be that I can be sent to any country and still find a way to keep my cool and survive.
This is real—like holding a weapon against harsh environments.
The ability to think independently, strip away ingrained perspectives, view problems without self-centeredness, find inner motivation, and so on.
Oh, and the most important: respect and equality, respecting others’ lives—no one is nobler than anyone else.
My perspective on the world has completely changed. Being abroad feels way freer and more broad-minded when looking at issues, without the heavy restrictions on the internet and speech.
I think the most important thing is breaking out of the mold that shapes your cognition. Studying abroad forces you to struggle and clash between two civilizations, two languages, and two societies.
Yes, whether you gain something depends on your own understanding, acceptance, and cognition.
After I came back, I happily accepted whatever people gave me, saying 'Great, thanks!' Then my mom almost knocked my head off for it.
The difference between low-context and high-context cultures.
Learning to be alone with yourself.
A completely unfamiliar country and social culture acts like an amplifier for your inner feelings.
People don’t have to always move upwards; they can also move in all directions.
Well said.
Support for the idea that no matter what, you can survive. Then coming back home really makes you feel life is full of unnoticed beauty.
So impressive.
Seeing people on Xiaohongshu still asking these kinds of questions instead of blindly labeling international students is really touching.
Yes, I share the same feelings as Ren.
A sincere question from someone who hasn’t studied abroad: aren’t those domestic migrant workers who say 'no matter what, you can survive' basically the same?
Because even if you leave your hometown in China, you’re still in the same cultural and language circle, so it’s hard to trigger thinking about different cultures.
It’s like being obsessed with prestigious schools, including Tsinghua and Peking University, it feels like everyone is pretty much the same.
No one seems to mention this, but I think abroad there’s a very respectful and open environment that lets you be an independent individual.
I did my undergrad and master’s abroad, and personally I feel there’s no knowledge you absolutely must get by studying abroad.
How different can knowledge really be? It’s definitely not that different. In other aspects, if you haven’t compared undergrad and master’s abroad, of course you won’t see the difference.
When I first went to a speaking workshop abroad, the host was a school staff member about 1.8m tall with purple dyed hair, smokey makeup, and all kinds of piercings.
Back home, I used to avoid people with big floral tattoos and never had the chance to interact with them, but after going abroad, my classmates all have big floral tattoos.
I'm not an overseas student, but ten years ago I was lucky enough to travel for over two months with two overseas student friends to two countries.
What does the last sentence mean?
The only thing I've learned is to live in the moment. Although I do get anxious about school and work, I don't habitually spend a long time drowning in pain.
The earlier you know, the better you understand which kind of life suits you.
Exactly.
It's very free, but this kind of freedom doesn't come from Western culture's idea of freedom; it comes from your identity as a foreigner temporarily living abroad.
I get this.
More charm and respect towards everyone, more empathy. Some people and things you might not understand yourself, but you respect their right to exist.
Critical thinking.
Critical thinking.
Chinese people stick together abroad, but back home, we're just scattered like loose sand.
What's important? The physical self is important. (I still don't have the courage to step out yet.)
Broadening horizons and independent living skills; the rest probably has nothing to do with studying abroad.

text: How to judge something? Many schools in mainland China forbid you from thinking about certain things. In Taiwan, because there's a bit of political freedom... it's possible. I've met many mainland people in both places who told me: Your ideas... are very dangerous.
Because different countries and cultures bring experiences, you learn to accept and respect differences, not to turn others into yourself.
Realizing that although every place is a pile of shit, every pile of shit is different.
The biggest change in cognition is realizing that nothing is owed to you, which leads to stopping demands and learning gratitude.
Of course, it's about broadening horizons, having more diverse ways of thinking about culture and disciplines, and accessing the academic resources of local big shots.
I took an elective course on gender, sexuality, and feminism.
Broaden your horizons. During studying abroad, you'll travel to many countries, experience different cultures, and learn to respect and embrace diversity.

The biggest gain from going abroad is understanding your own country and culture. Before going, you might not think your culture is special, but after going, you'll realize how rich and brilliant it is, and you'll start seriously studying your culture and history. Also, you develop the ability to see things from different perspectives; many issues aren't just black or white.
You get to engage with the top minds and academic attitudes.
Learn how to have conversations and ask questions, how to communicate and debate with others, and how to find and verify various information.
This experience taught me not to jump to conclusions based on a single news event or a snippet from social media.
The shift from an institutional culture to an outside-institution culture.
From being spoon-fed to learning how to feed yourself, from passive learning to active learning.

Confidence to challenge authority.

Everything is trash, no environment is right or wrong; it all depends on what you want.
